summary: This memo outlines the problems of moving from informal 8-bit messages to MIME, and suggests an approach that keeps the cost of the move small for the Internet mail system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people had been sending special characters in mail in an informal way. This paper discusses how to switch everyone to the proper system without breaking things.

questions: moving from non-mime 8bit mail to mime
how to transition from 8-bit mail to mime
subtitle: Moving email from informal 8-bit extensions to the standard MIME protocol

tldr.problem: SMTP was limited to 7-bit ASCII, but as the Internet grew international, people used ad-hoc methods to send 8-bit characters (special accents, non-Latin scripts). These informal approaches created compatibility problems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC outlines how to upgrade to the formal MIME and 8bit-SMTP standards using gateway servers that can convert old-style 8-bit messages to proper MIME format with character set declarations.
tldr.outcome: The upgrade path allows old systems and new MIME-aware systems to coexist, using the 'unknown-8bit' charset as a temporary label when the exact character set cannot be determined.

today: RFC 1428 is informational and describes a transition period from the early 1990s. Today, MIME is the universal standard for email, and the ad-hoc 8-bit approaches described here are obsolete. However, the RFC remains historically relevant as documentation of the Internet's shift toward internationalization.

sections.title: The Challenge of Non-ASCII Mail
sections.content:
RFC 821 defined SMTP to transport only 7-bit US-ASCII characters. As the Internet expanded globally, people wanted to send messages in their own languages and character sets. Rather than wait for a standard upgrade, many implementers created ad-hoc 8-bit extensions: they simply sent 8-bit data over SMTP and hoped the receiving system would understand it.

The problem is that 8-bit data means nothing without context: eight bits could represent an ISO 8859-1 character, a Japanese character using ISO 2022 encoding, or something else entirely. When messages traveled across different ad-hoc systems, characters would be garbled or lost.
sections.plainLanguage: People were sending secret codes that only worked if both friends used the same secret code. When mail went to someone using a different code, it became garbage.

sections.title: The Interoperability Problem
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six main scenarios where sender and receiver systems have different capabilities:

  • 7bit to 7bit/8bit/MIME: Works unchanged with out-of-band agreement on character set.
  • 8bit (ad-hoc) to 7bit: Bits get stripped, corrupting the text. Unreadable unless the language is close to ASCII.
  • 8bit (ad-hoc) to 8bit (ad-hoc): Works only if both sites use the same character set informally.
  • 8bit (ad-hoc) to MIME/ESMTP: The focus of this RFC. Requires gateway intervention and character set identification.
  • MIME/ESMTP to 7bit: The sender must encode as base-64 or quoted-printable (appearing garbled), or the gateway must know the receiver's capabilities.
  • MIME/ESMTP to MIME/ESMTP: Works if both support the declared character set.
sections.plainLanguage: Different combinations of old and new systems cause different problems. Some work fine, some lose information, and some need a helper to translate.

sections.title: The Upgrade Path Using Gateways
sections.content:
The solution uses gateway servers positioned between old and new systems. When a gateway receives an old-style 8-bit message bound for a MIME/ESMTP receiver, it converts the message by:

  • Adding a MIME-Version: 1.0 header.
  • Adding a Content-Type: Text/Plain; Charset=... header, specifying the character set if known.
  • Adding a Content-Transfer-Encoding header to indicate whether the 8-bit data can pass as-is.
  • Encoding any non-ASCII characters in the RFC 822 headers themselves using quoted-printable or base-64 per RFC 1342.
  • Recording the conversion in a Received header trace clause like convert rfc822-to-8bit.

Sites can upgrade their entire outgoing mail en masse if they use a single character set organization-wide, simply by wrapping all outgoing messages with the appropriate MIME headers.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper server reads the old message and slaps a label on it saying 'This is 8-bit ISO-8859-1' or whatever the language is, so the new system knows how to read it.

sections.title: The unknown-8bit Charset
sections.content:
Often, a gateway cannot determine what character set a legacy 8-bit message uses. For this case, the RFC defines a special charset value: unknown-8bit.

This is not a real character set; it simply tells the receiving MIME system 'we found 8-bit data but have no idea what it is.' The receiving mail reader can then show the raw octets, prompt the user to guess the encoding, or apply heuristics to detect the likely character set. The key is that the message is no longer silent mystery—the receiver knows to look at it as raw 8-bit data, not as garbled ASCII.

This approach keeps the cost of transition low: gateways do not need to implement sophisticated character set detection. Sites that can identify their local character set tag messages properly; others use unknown-8bit as a placeholder, and humans can intervene.
sections.plainLanguage: If the helper doesn't know what language the message is in, it puts a label that says 'unknown language here'—better than pretending it's ASCII and mangling it.

sections.title: Practical Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that the real-world interoperability challenge is complex. Messages may encode non-ASCII in multiple ways: ISO 8859 character sets (with the high bit set), ISO 2022 escape sequences (which switch between 7-bit and 14-bit encodings), or proprietary PC character sets.

The gateway approach succeeds only if the original message's character set can be inferred. This may be possible from:

  • Site configuration (if the gateway serves a known domain).
  • The Received headers and routing information (which may hint at the sender's region).
  • Heuristics applied to the byte patterns (e.g., valid ISO 8859-1 sequences versus invalid ones).
  • User input (when the gateway cannot decide, it may query a human administrator).

The trade-off is simplicity versus precision: a gateway that always uses unknown-8bit is easy but unhelpful; one that tries to guess may make errors. This memo advocates for best-effort labeling without over-engineering the detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting old messages to the new system takes some guesswork, but even an uncertain label is better than no label at all.
